addedResources.name: NVIDIA CUDA Pro Tips: grid-stride loops and vectorized memory access
addedResources.use: Read the grid-stride SAXPY loop and its scalability and debugging discussion (April 22, 2013), plus the scalar-copy SASS and vector-type alignment discussion in Increase Performance with Vectorized Memory Access (August 4, 2025). Skip the latter article's full vector-copy kernels: their tail-thread condition can omit remainders. These fill the pool's grid-stride and vector-width coverage gaps.

addedResources.name: CUDA Binary Utilities 13.4
addedResources.use: Sections 1.1 to 1.2, 2.1.1 to 2.1.3, 3.1.1 and 3.1.4 for cubin extraction, resource reports and line-correlated SASS. The existing compiler and PTX references lack a worked binary-tool workflow.

addedResources.name: PyTorch custom C++/CUDA operators and CUDA semantics
addedResources.use: Custom C++ and CUDA Operators: build system, backend registration, Testing an operator and mutable schema; CUDA semantics 2.14: CUDA streams. These fill the native tensor-boundary gap in the CUDA-only pool. Stop before fake-kernel and autograd implementation; harden the tutorial's CUDA example for empty inputs, same-device checks, device guards, indexing width and launch errors.

units.title: Host, device, kernels, index mapping and explicit device memory
outcomes: Map one- and two-dimensional launches to distinct output elements, including edge threads.
Implement explicit device allocation, input copies, a kernel launch, result validation and cleanup.
Explain which work runs on the host and why a successful launch is not evidence of completion.
units.why: Every kernel starts with a mapping and an ownership boundary. Getting those right lets later experiments change performance without changing the operation.

next.note: Map the logical threads onto warp and SM resources.

study.title: PMPP, 4th edition: kernels, copies and multidimensional mapping
CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2: explicit memory and error handling

focus: A grid contains blocks; each block contains threads. Compute row and column separately, then use the storage layout to form the element offset.
Allocation and copy sizes are bytes, not element counts. Keep ownership of each allocation on the host and release it on every error path.
Kernel launch is asynchronous. Check `cudaGetLastError()` after launching and check the completion operation before consuming results.
units.reproduce: From a blank CUDA C++ program, add 1003 single-precision elements with inputs `a[i] = float(i)` and `b[i] = 1.0f`. Use four blocks of 256 threads, explicit allocation and copies, and a bounds check. All 1003 results must equal `float(i + 1)` exactly; 21 launched threads must perform no memory access. Check every CUDA return value and free all allocations.
traps: Dereferencing an ordinary `cudaMalloc` device pointer on the CPU. Passing the pointer to a runtime API is not the same as accessing its pointee.
Using the grid width instead of the tensor row stride to flatten a two-dimensional address.
Treating a successful launch check as proof that the kernel has finished without an execution error.

selfTest.q: Why does the 1003-element launch need a guard even though the grid covers the input?
selfTest.a: Four blocks contain 1024 threads. The last 21 have indices outside the allocation; covering the input does not make those addresses valid.

selfTest.q: Does using a two-dimensional grid make the input tensor two-dimensional in memory?
selfTest.a: No. Launch coordinates and storage layout are separate. The kernel must compute an address from the tensor's actual layout.

selfTest.q: What must happen before the host checks the output?
selfTest.a: Kernel writes must complete and the results must be accessible to the host. In this explicit-memory program, check synchronization and the device-to-host copy before reading the host buffer.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `kernellab` explicit-memory vector-add baseline, two-dimensional index map and independent host-reference tests.
units.stopWhen: Your vector-add baseline passes lengths 0, 1, 31, 32, 33 and 1003, with zero length handled on the host, and you can draw a rectangular launch's address map without running it.

fit.note: PMPP supplies the mapping and ownership first pass; the current CUDA guide supplies asynchronous error checks, and the section mini-project supplies implementation practice.

units.title: Warps, SMs, block residency and latency hiding
outcomes: Predict warp membership and inactive positions for multidimensional and nonmultiple-of-32 blocks.
Distinguish resident, eligible and issuing warps, and explain how scheduling hides dependency latency.
Explain why a block stays on one SM but its warps do not all execute at once.
units.why: A launch describes logical parallelism, not simultaneous execution. Latency hiding depends on ready work at the scheduler, not just the number of threads launched.

next.note: Calculate how many of these warps can be resident.

study.title: PMPP, 4th edition: block and warp scheduling
MIT 6.S894 Fall 2025 Lab 2: FMA latency and instruction-level parallelism
study.locator: Background: A Closer Look at the Hardware; Part 0 (Prelab): Instruction Latency of an FMA, through Prelab Question 3
study.depth: Use the GPU material only. The RTX 4000 Ada scheduler counts and clocks describe the course machine, not your GPU. Stop before Using ILP in a Simple Program.

focus: Linearize within a block with the x coordinate fastest. Warps never combine threads from different blocks.
All warps of a block reside on one SM. A normal launch does not promise a particular block-to-SM assignment or block order.
A resident warp can be stalled. Another eligible warp or independent instructions within the same warp can cover the wait without reducing the instruction's dependency latency.
units.reproduce: Draw the warp map for `dim3 block(16, 3, 1)`. Warp 0 contains both complete rows with y coordinates 0 and 1; warp 1 contains the 16 threads of row 2 and has 16 unused positions. Two such blocks allocate four warps, not three. Verify the map with a kernel that writes each thread's linear index, warp index and lane index to a separate output slot.
traps: Counting CUDA cores as simultaneously resident threads. Residency and execution throughput are different limits.
Assuming one block per SM because the grid has as many blocks as SMs. Correctness cannot depend on that scheduling choice.
Calling an independent-chain benchmark's elapsed cycles per FMA the latency of a dependent FMA. It measures a different quantity.

selfTest.q: Can the final 16 threads of two 48-thread blocks share one warp?
selfTest.a: No. Each block independently allocates two warps; the unused positions of its final warp cannot be filled by another block.

selfTest.q: Why can an SM stall with many resident warps?
selfTest.a: All those warps may be waiting on dependencies, memory or synchronization, leaving no eligible instruction to issue.

selfTest.q: Does interleaving independent FMA chains make a dependent FMA finish sooner?
selfTest.a: No. It exposes independent work during the wait and may improve throughput; the producer-to-consumer dependency latency is unchanged.

practice.name: MIT 6.S894 Fall 2025 Lab 2: FMA prelab Questions 1 to 3
practice.note: Build locally with `nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_86 fma_latency.cu -o fma_latency`, not Telerun. Use long dependent chains, consume their results, and inspect SASS for retained FMAs. Reset inputs between variants and use bounded finite values. The starter prints whole-snippet cycles, so divide by the retained FMA count and account for timer overhead. Repeat interleaved trials and report medians, hardware and toolkit; no course latency or speedup is a target. This is an investigative lab, not an autograded correctness suite.

units.stopWhen: You predict the two-block warp map correctly and can explain the prelab's dependent-chain and independent-chain measurements using the actual SASS, without claiming a fixed speedup.

fit.note: PMPP covers formation and residency; the bounded Lab 2 FMA prelab adds a named dependency-versus-throughput experiment on the learner's own GPU.

units.title: Occupancy limits, registers, spills and launch resources
outcomes: Derive resident-block limits from threads, warps, blocks, registers and shared memory.
Validate a compiled kernel's launch resources with device properties, compiler reports and the occupancy API.
Sweep block size and resource use, keeping correctness and explaining why higher occupancy need not reduce time.
units.why: Registers and shared memory can save traffic while reducing residency. Occupancy is a resource bound to reconcile with measurements, not an optimization score.

next.note: Find the resource allocation in the final machine code.

study.title: PMPP, 4th edition: resource partitioning
CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide 13.4: occupancy and local memory
study.depth: Do not adopt Section 11.1's assertion that low occupancy always degrades performance. Section 11.3 itself explains that sufficient instruction-level parallelism can cover latency at low occupancy. Skip historical calculator screenshots.

study.title: CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2: launch and memory resource limits

focus: Calculate whole resident blocks, then resident warps divided by the SM's warp maximum. Include every resource limit and allocation granularity; a continuous bytes-per-thread estimate is not enough.
Read `numRegs` and static shared bytes from compiled-kernel attributes. Add dynamic shared bytes supplied at launch; compare the estimate with `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor`.
Local memory is thread-private device memory, not an on-chip scratchpad. A local array is not necessarily a spill; inspect the compiler's spill report and final code.

Compare event-timed, correctness-checked variants with warmup and interleaved repeated trials. If counters are permitted, inspect Nsight Compute's Occupancy section; otherwise report theoretical occupancy and timings separately.
units.reproduce: Derive TensorTonic's first occupancy example with 100 threads per block, warp size 32, 64 registers per effective thread and 2048 shared bytes per block. The supplied SM limits are 1024 effective threads, 32 warps, 16 blocks, 32768 registers and 49152 shared bytes. Its simplified model allocates four warps and 128 effective threads per block. Registers permit four blocks, hence 16 resident warps and 50% occupancy. Then sweep a compiled vector-add kernel at 128, 256 and 512 threads, with 0, 16384 and 32768 dynamic shared bytes, recording the API's block limit and event-time median rather than predicting a speed ranking.
traps: Using `sharedMemPerBlock` or `regsPerBlock` as the SM capacity. Per-block legality and per-SM residency are separate checks.
Forcing a register cap and assuming the reduced register count is a free improvement. Spills or recomputation can erase the residency gain.
Equating theoretical occupancy with achieved occupancy or the fraction of cycles doing useful work. A small grid or stalled warps can leave the machine underused.

selfTest.q: Why is TensorTonic's first example limited to four blocks rather than eight?
selfTest.a: Each block uses 8192 registers in the stated model. The 32768-register budget allows four blocks even though thread and warp budgets allow eight.

selfTest.q: Can a declared local array be implemented in registers?
selfTest.a: Yes, if the compiler can scalarize its accesses and resources permit. A source declaration does not prove a particular final placement.

selfTest.q: Why might allocating unused dynamic shared memory change time?
selfTest.a: It changes residency and possibly the L1/shared-memory carveout without changing useful arithmetic. Those effects can change latency hiding and caching, so this is not a perfectly isolated occupancy-only control.

practice.name: TensorTonic: GPU Occupancy Calculator
practice.locator: Implement `gpu_occupancy`; work its three public cases: register-limited, shared-memory-limited and oversized block
practice.note: This free problem deliberately omits hardware allocation rounding beyond whole warps. Solve that stated model, not an undocumented approximation to an actual SM. The section mini-project covers the compiled-kernel sweep, spill diagnosis and per-block launch validation; compare the real kernel with the CUDA occupancy API.

units.stopWhen: Your calculator matches the public examples, and your real-kernel sweep identifies each limiting resource, reconciles API versus hand estimates and retains timings without treating occupancy as speed.

fit.note: PMPP and CUDA cover the analytical and compiled-kernel resource models; TensorTonic supplies named simplified-model practice and `kernellab` supplies the measured sweep.

units.title: Global memory, caches, transactions and coalescing
outcomes: Derive the aligned memory sectors touched by each warp instruction, including offsets, strides and access widths.
Distinguish useful bytes, requested sectors, cache hits and traffic reaching device memory.
Measure paired access patterns and explain discrepancies between sector predictions and elapsed time.
units.why: Threads that are adjacent in a tensor need not request adjacent bytes. The address pattern of each instruction determines coalescing; caches then determine how much of that traffic reaches device memory.

next.note: Use a shared-memory tile to repair a strided global access.

study.title: PMPP, 4th edition: coalescing and memory latency
study.locator: Section 6.1, Figures 6.1 to 6.4; Section 6.2 through Figure 6.8
study.depth: Stop before the toy channel assignment in Figure 6.9. Use CUDA's sector model below rather than treating a DRAM burst as the transaction unit of every GPU.

study.title: CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide 13.4: aligned, offset and strided accesses
CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2: device caches
NVIDIA: vectorized memory access, August 4, 2025
study.locator: Opening scalar copy kernel and SASS, then the vector-type and alignment discussion through the aligned `int2` pointer-offset example
study.depth: Stop before the structure example and full vector-copy kernels. Their remainder handler relies on a thread whose index can lie outside the launched grid, so it can skip the tail. Treat performance improvements as hypotheses, not guarantees.

focus: For compute capability 6.0 and later, count distinct aligned 32-byte sectors touched by the active lanes of one instruction. Permuting the same addresses does not change that count.
Count every byte of a wide access, including sector crossings. A wider instruction may reduce instruction count without reducing useful bytes or aggregate sectors for the same work.
L1 is local to an SM and L2 is shared across SMs. Requested sectors are not measured DRAM bytes; cache reuse can make the timing penalty smaller than a per-warp sector ratio.
A base allocation's alignment does not guarantee an offset view's alignment. Validate the address and tail before using `int2` or `int4` loads.
units.reproduce: For one fully active 32-lane warp, derive the sector counts for four-byte loads from byte addresses \(4\ell\), \(4\ell+4\) and \(32\ell\), where \(0\leq\ell<32\) and the base address is 32-byte aligned. Obtain 4, 5 and 32 sectors, with unique useful-byte fractions 100%, 80% and 12.5%. Implement a byte-interval union counter and verify the predictions. In `kernellab`, compare bounds-safe offset and stride copy variants with an independent reference and event timings; do not convert those sector ratios directly into speedups.
traps: Calling a 128-byte cache line one 32-byte sector. TensorTonic's configurable line model and the CUDA sector model use different transaction units.
Counting only starting addresses for vector accesses. A load can touch several sectors.
Calling a copy memory-bound from its source alone. Small arrays can be launch-limited, and cache-resident arrays have a different traffic boundary.

selfTest.q: If lanes reverse the order of 32 adjacent four-byte words at an aligned base, does the sector count change?
selfTest.a: No. The same four sectors are touched; coalescing depends on the address set, not lane order.

selfTest.q: Why can an offset copy lose less time than its five-versus-four sector ratio suggests?
selfTest.a: Adjacent warps can reuse overlapping sectors in cache. The per-warp request count is not the total traffic reaching DRAM.

selfTest.q: A warp loads one consecutive 16-byte object per lane from a 32-byte-aligned base. How many sectors cover its byte range?
selfTest.a: Sixteen sectors cover 512 bytes. Wider per-lane loads do not make that byte range fit in four sectors.

practice.name: TensorTonic: Global-Memory Coalescing Counter
practice.locator: Implement `coalescing_analysis`; work the adjacent-word, separated-line and line-crossing public cases
practice.note: This free problem counts each requested byte once even where lanes overlap, with a default 128-byte line. Solve its stated model, then repeat your own cases with `cache_line_bytes=32` for the CUDA sector analysis. Its line-crossing case is an abstract byte interval, not permission to issue a misaligned typed CUDA load. The section mini-project covers the paired GPU copies and timings.

units.stopWhen: Your counter handles overlaps and crossings, the three sector predictions agree with your derivation, and your paired-copy report separates requested sectors from measured time and any unavailable DRAM counters.

fit.note: The pool covers coalescing and caches but lacks a focused vector-width and alignment locator; the opened NVIDIA vector-access article fills that gap, with its faulty tail kernels excluded.

units.title: Shared-memory banks, conflicts, padding and the constant cache
outcomes: Predict shared-memory bank IDs and conflict degree for scalar word accesses, including broadcasts.
Derive when padding a row stride removes column-access conflicts.
Choose between shared memory, constant memory and read-only global loads for a stated access pattern.
units.why: On-chip storage does not make every access pattern efficient. Bank mapping and the number of distinct constant addresses within a warp matter as much as placement.

next.note: Apply the bank derivation to a padded transpose tile.

study.title: PMPP, 4th edition: memory types
CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2: banks, broadcast and padding
study.locator: Section 2.3.4.2 before the transpose example; Section 2.3.4.2.2, Shared Memory Bank Conflicts, Figures 17 and 18
study.depth: Skip the full transpose implementation in 2.3.4.2.1 here. Derive the bank map before implementing a transpose in the primitives section.

study.title: CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide 13.4: constant-cache access
CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2: read-only global loads
study.depth: Read only the read-only-load contract, not the list of cache-control intrinsics.

focus: For aligned scalar 32-bit accesses on the 32-bank model, the bank is \(\lfloor a/4\rfloor\bmod32\), with byte address \(a\). Count distinct words per bank, not just requesting lanes.
Same-word reads can broadcast. Different words in the same bank conflict; same-address competing writes are not a safe broadcast-based algorithm.
A row-major tile with 32 columns gives column accesses a 32-word stride. Padding to 33 columns changes the bank stride to one modulo 32.

Constant memory favors few distinct addresses per warp. A read-only global pointer is not a `__constant__` allocation, and a read-only cache is not coherent with writes to that data during the kernel.
units.reproduce: For a full warp of aligned four-byte shared-memory reads, compute banks for word indices \(\ell s\) at strides \(s\in\{1,2,3,32,33\}\). Obtain conflict degrees 1, 2, 1, 32 and 1, assuming distinct words and one scalar access per lane. Then replace all addresses with the same word: the reads broadcast with degree 1. Explain why the same calculation does not prove a general bank rule for vector or 64-bit accesses.
traps: Applying the scalar bank-conflict rule across separate hardware transactions of a wide instruction. Analyze the actual instruction's transaction groups.
Adding padding without recalculating addresses and shared-memory capacity. A changed stride can fix one access and alter another.
Choosing constant memory just because the data never changes. Many distinct addresses in one warp serialize constant-cache requests.

selfTest.q: Why does word stride 3 avoid conflicts in this 32-bank scalar model?
selfTest.a: Three is coprime to 32, so multiplication by three modulo 32 visits every bank once across the 32 lanes.

selfTest.q: Four lanes read byte addresses 0, 128, 256 and 384. Is this a broadcast?
selfTest.a: No. They read four different words in bank 0, making a four-way conflict in the stated model.

selfTest.q: Would a small lookup table with one distinct lookup per lane necessarily favor constant memory?
selfTest.a: No. Constant requests serialize by distinct address within a warp. Read-only global access may be a better hypothesis, which still needs measurement.

practice.name: TensorTonic: Shared-Memory Bank Conflict Analyzer
practice.locator: Implement `bank_conflict_analysis`; work all three public cases: adjacent words, four-way conflict and same-address broadcast
practice.note: This free problem counts distinct addresses per bank and returns a degree for each lane. Treat it as a scalar-read model. Add your own full-warp stride and padded-tile cases; the section mini-project covers paired conflicting and conflict-free kernels.

units.stopWhen: Your analyzer passes the public examples and your five stride cases, and you can defend a memory-space choice from the warp's addresses without calling all read-only data constant memory.

fit.note: PMPP's memory first pass plus CUDA's exact bank, constant-cache and read-only-load locators cover the unit; TensorTonic provides named analytical practice.

units.title: Divergence, predication, grid-stride loops and bounds
outcomes: Predict divergent paths and useful active lanes for a warp, including a partial tail.
Implement a bounds-safe grid-stride map with zero-size handling and overflow-aware indexing.
Use generated code to distinguish branches from predicated instructions rather than guessing from source syntax.
units.why: Bounds checks are part of correctness, not an optional performance cost. A grid-stride loop decouples coverage from launch size while preserving adjacent-lane addressing within each iteration.

next.note: Keep bounds and divergent control compatible with synchronization.

study.title: PMPP, 4th edition: control divergence
CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide 13.4: branches and predication
NVIDIA: flexible kernels with grid-stride loops
study.locator: Monolithic SAXPY kernel, grid-stride SAXPY kernel, Scalability and thread reuse, and Debugging

focus: Divergence is within a warp. Different uniform paths in different warps need not serialize each other as divergent paths of one warp do.
A source `if` may become a branch, a select or predicated instructions. Inspect the final code before describing the machine's control flow.
A grid-stride loop starts at the global thread index and increments by the total grid thread count. Each element belongs to one residue class, so coverage is complete without overlapping writes.
Handle an empty input on the host rather than launching a zero-block grid. Promote operands before index multiplication and define a size limit that also prevents loop-increment overflow.
units.reproduce: Convert the vector-add baseline to a grid-stride loop. For 1003 elements and a one-block, 128-thread launch, thread 0 handles indices 0, 128, 256, 384, 512, 640, 768 and 896; thread 127 handles seven indices ending at 895. Validate every result against the host reference, then repeat with a one-thread launch and lengths 0, 1, 31, 32 and 33. Use the exact integer-valued single-precision inputs from the programming-model unit, so equality is exact here, not a general floating-point promise.
traps: Using block size alone as the loop stride in a multi-block grid. Blocks then overlap work.
Removing the tail guard to avoid divergence. Invalid memory access cannot be traded for speed.
Assuming a serial GPU launch reproduces all CPU floating-point arithmetic bit for bit. Contraction, precision and operation order can still differ.

selfTest.q: Does `threadIdx.x < 32` diverge a block with 128 threads?
selfTest.a: It gives different paths to different warps, but each warp's predicate is uniform. It is not within-warp divergence for this one-dimensional launch.

selfTest.q: Why is a grid-stride map complete even when the grid is smaller than the input?
selfTest.a: Every valid index has a unique remainder modulo the total grid thread count. That thread reaches the index after a finite number of loop increments.

selfTest.q: Is converting the completed index product to a wide type sufficient to avoid overflow?
selfTest.a: No. The multiplication can overflow before conversion. Promote an operand before multiplication and also check the maximum supported size and increment.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `kernellab` grid-stride map, odd and empty tails, paired uniform and divergent control kernels, and source-to-SASS control-flow annotations.
units.stopWhen: Your grid-stride map passes the stated lengths with both launch sizes, and you predict lane activity for a new predicate before checking its generated control flow.

fit.note: The pool covers divergence but has no focused grid-stride implementation locator; the verified NVIDIA SAXPY article fills that coverage gap, with `kernellab` providing edge-case practice.

units.title: Synchronization scopes, atomics and memory ordering
outcomes: Choose warp, block, cluster or device coordination from the communicating participants.
Distinguish atomicity, memory ordering and barriers, and derive a release/acquire publication relation.
Identify a synchronization hazard caused by divergent participation or inter-block scheduling.
units.why: An atomic flag is not automatically a publication protocol. Correct coordination needs both a matching scope and an ordering relation for the payload.

next.note: Place block barriers around a shared-memory tile's producer and consumer phases.

study.title: CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2: scope and atomic order
study.depth: Read the scoped atomic definitions, not the full producer-consumer sample: its shared flag is not initialized. Cluster and grid cooperative programming are later implementation work.

study.title: CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2: barriers and participating lanes
study.depth: Skip the Section 5.4.4.1 example labelled valid behavior: `shared_data[128 - threadIdx.x]` addresses index 128 for thread 0 in a 128-element array.

study.title: CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2: memory model and publication
study.depth: Trace the message-passing ordering, but do not use an inter-block spin wait as a general grid barrier: waiting resident blocks can prevent a producer block from being scheduled.

focus: Scope identifies which threads an atomic operation can coordinate. Device scope does not turn the operation into a device-wide barrier; system scope has additional type, alignment and platform prerequisites.

A release store publishes earlier payload writes to a consumer whose acquire load reads that store, provided both operations have sufficient scope. A relaxed atomic update alone orders no unrelated payload.

A block barrier requires block-uniform participation and orders participating threads' relevant prior accesses. A warp barrier requires a correct participant mask; implicit lockstep is not a synchronization contract.
Initialization must happen before flag use. Separate correctness of memory ordering from forward progress: an ordered spin loop can still deadlock under an unsuitable launch.
units.reproduce: Draw and then implement a two-warp, one-block publication test. Thread 0 initializes a shared integer flag to zero; all 64 threads execute a block barrier. Thread 0 writes payload 42 and uses `cuda::atomic_ref<int, cuda::thread_scope_block>` to release-store flag 1. Thread 32 acquire-loads until it sees 1, then writes the payload to an output slot. The host must observe 42 after checked completion. Explain the initialization barrier and release/acquire happens-before path separately; do not move this protocol to arbitrary blocks without a forward-progress argument.
traps: Putting a block barrier inside a lane-dependent bounds condition. Guard memory operations while keeping required barrier participation uniform.
Using `volatile` or a memory fence as a substitute for an atomic flag and a matching acquire operation.
Calling a successful stress test proof of a racy protocol. A missing ordering relation can remain invisible on a particular run.

selfTest.q: Does a relaxed atomic increment publish an unrelated ordinary write?
selfTest.a: No. It makes the increment atomic at its scope, but supplies no release/acquire relation for the unrelated payload.

selfTest.q: Can a device-scoped flag safely coordinate host reads on every platform?
selfTest.a: No. Host coordination needs a supported system-scoped mechanism and compatible memory, or explicit stream completion and transfer.

selfTest.q: Why can a correctly ordered inter-block spin protocol hang?
selfTest.a: Waiting blocks can occupy the available residency slots while the producer remains unscheduled. Memory ordering does not guarantee block scheduling or a global barrier.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `kernellab` initialized block-local publication test, shared-memory producer/consumer barriers and a written scope-and-progress audit. Deliberately racy variants are analyzed, not treated as valid timed kernels.
units.stopWhen: Your publication test returns 42, and you can trace its initialization, synchronization scope and happens-before relation without relying on observed lockstep.

fit.note: The current CUDA guide supplies precise scope, barrier and ordering locators; defective examples are excluded and the mini-project provides bounded implementation practice.

units.title: From CUDA source to PTX, cubin and SASS
outcomes: Explain host compilation, PTX generation, offline assembly and driver JIT without calling PTX the final machine code.
Build and inspect explicit virtual and real architecture targets, recording toolchain and resource use.
Connect a source-level hypothesis to retained SASS instructions and a correctness-checked timing comparison.
units.why: The compiler can remove, fuse, predicate or scalarize the code you intended to measure. Binary inspection makes the experiment about the instructions that actually execute.

next.note: Package compatible code images and select only supported features at runtime.

study.title: CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2: compiler trajectory and targets
CUDA Binary Utilities 13.4: resource reports and disassembly
study.depth: Use command examples and line correlation only; skip control-flow graph tooling and instruction tables for architectures other than your target.

study.title: PTX ISA 9.4: goals, state spaces and module directives
study.locator: Sections 1.2 (Goals of PTX), 5.1 to 5.1.7 (state spaces, including `.reg`, `.param`, `.global`, `.local` and `.shared`) and 11.1.1 to 11.1.3 (`.version`, `.target` and `.address_size`)
study.depth: Read these sections against your own `map.ptx`: with CUDA 13.4, `-arch=compute_86 -ptx` emits `.version 9.4` and `.target sm_86`, kernel arguments in `.param` and virtual `.reg` registers. Skip the instruction reference beyond the loads, stores and FMA your kernel uses.

focus: A virtual `compute_86` target defines the PTX feature set; real `sm_86` code is assembled machine code. A fat binary can carry several cubins and PTX for eligible JIT fallback.
Save compiler version, flags, PTX, cubin resource reports and SASS together. `-lineinfo` aids correlation without the optimization changes caused by device debugging with `-G`.
PTX registers are virtual and do not equal allocated hardware registers. Use `ptxas` reports, kernel attributes and final binary resource information.
Annotate global loads/stores, bounds handling, FMA instructions and any local loads/stores in the final code. A source expression is not a guaranteed instruction sequence.
units.reproduce: For the bounded grid-stride map, run `nvcc -O3 -lineinfo -arch=sm_86 -Xptxas=-v map.cu -o map`, `nvcc -O3 -arch=compute_86 -ptx map.cu -o map.ptx`, and `nvcc -O3 -lineinfo -arch=sm_86 -cubin map.cu -o map.cubin`. Inspect with `cuobjdump --dump-sass --dump-resource-usage map` and `nvdisasm --print-line-info map.cubin`. These are the local RTX 3050 targets; choose matching targets on another device. Locate the retained index calculation, tail handling and stores, then validate and event-time the executable. Report actual registers and spills without assuming a fixed allocation or speedup.
traps: Counting PTX instructions as hardware issue cost. Assembly and JIT can transform them.
Benchmarking a `-G` build and generalizing its register use or time to the optimized build.
Inspecting a different architecture image or stale executable from the one measured. Keep artifact identities and commands in the evidence manifest.

selfTest.q: Does shipping only an `sm_86` cubin guarantee execution on every later GPU?
selfTest.a: No. Cubin compatibility is constrained; a different major architecture generally needs its own compatible image or eligible PTX fallback.

selfTest.q: Why might source multiplication plus addition appear as one instruction?
selfTest.a: The compiler can contract it to an FMA, subject to compilation rules. Inspect SASS and account for the changed rounding when comparing references.

selfTest.q: Can a kernel with many PTX register names use few physical registers?
selfTest.a: Yes. Virtual-register lifetimes can share physical registers after optimization and allocation. The final resource report is the relevant count.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `kernellab` source/PTX/cubin/SASS evidence bundle, compiler resource table and one disassembly-backed paired timing hypothesis.
units.stopWhen: Your evidence bundle ties the validated executable to its targets, resource report and annotated final instructions, and distinguishes offline cubin execution from possible PTX JIT.

fit.note: The pool explains compilation and PTX but lacks binary-tool command and line-correlation locators; official CUDA Binary Utilities supplies that reference gap.

units.title: Native extension contracts: shapes, strides, aliasing and layout
outcomes: Specify and enforce shape, dtype, device, stride, alignment and aliasing preconditions at a native tensor boundary.
Launch on the input device's current framework stream while preserving tensor ownership and lifetime.
Test valid views, empty inputs and rejected inputs against an independent framework reference.
units.why: A correct standalone kernel can become incorrect when passed a tensor view or launched on the wrong stream. The wrapper is part of the algorithm's correctness contract.

focus: Choose a layout policy: reject unsupported strides, index actual strides, or explicitly normalize inputs with `contiguous()`. Include normalization cost in end-to-end measurements.

For a simple out-of-place map, accept same-shape float32 CUDA inputs on the same device, allocate a fresh output, and define whether gradients are supported. Do not promise broadcasting or mutation accidentally.
A view's data pointer includes its storage offset but says nothing about subsequent strides or vector alignment. Validate vector alignment independently and provide a scalar tail or fallback.
Guard the input device and use its current framework stream, not an assumed default stream. If work crosses streams, execution dependencies and caching-allocator lifetime need separate handling.
units.reproduce: Build an inference-only out-of-place float32 vector-add extension. Require equal shapes and one CUDA device, explicitly normalize noncontiguous inputs, guard that device, use its current stream and wide grid-stride indices, return an empty output without a zero-block launch, and check launch errors. Compare with `a + b` on lengths 0, 1, 31, 32, 33 and 1003, a transposed two-dimensional view and a contiguous view offset by one element. Reject mismatched shapes, dtypes, devices and gradient-requiring inputs under the stated inference contract. Confirm fresh output storage, unchanged inputs and non-default-stream execution with an explicit dependency before host validation.
traps: Using `numel()` and a raw pointer as proof of contiguous layout. A transposed tensor has the same element count but different strides.
Adding `__restrict__` while permitting output-input overlap. The promise must match the actual access and aliasing contract; two read-only inputs aliasing each other is a different case.
Synchronizing the whole device on every call to hide stream bugs. Preserve asynchronous behavior and synchronize only at the test or measurement boundary.

selfTest.q: A float32 allocation is aligned to 16 bytes. Is its view starting one element later safe for an `int4` load?
selfTest.a: No. The four-byte offset breaks 16-byte alignment. Use an aligned path or scalar accesses instead.

selfTest.q: Does `record_stream` make a consuming stream wait for a producer?
selfTest.a: No. It tells the allocator about use on another stream. A stream wait or event establishes execution order; lifetime tracking is separate.

selfTest.q: Does passing `opcheck` prove the arithmetic and gradients are correct?
selfTest.a: No. It checks registration behavior. Use an independent numerical reference and, when gradients are supported later, separate gradient tests.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `kernellab` native vector-add wrapper, explicit inference contract, view/alignment tests, rejection matrix and non-default-stream lifetime checks. Fake-tensor and autograd integration remain later work.
units.stopWhen: Your wrapper passes the valid-input reference matrix and rejects unsupported inputs before launch, with documented layout, aliasing, stream and lifetime policies.

fit.note: The CUDA-only pool has no framework tensor-boundary or allocator-lifetime locator; official PyTorch custom-operator and CUDA-stream documentation fills the coverage and currency gaps.

units.title: Compute capability, feature detection and fallback paths
outcomes: Query device and kernel limits and distinguish feature support from launch legality and binary compatibility.
Implement a deterministic dispatch decision with a validated baseline fallback and an explicit unsupported reason.
Exercise both dispatch branches without claiming that an unavailable hardware feature was executed.
units.why: Compilation for a new target does not make a feature available on an older device. A portable library needs an observable decision and a baseline whose correctness does not depend on the optimization.

next.note: Keep a validated ordinary-kernel path while introducing tiled and architecture-specific variants.

study.title: CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2: cubin and PTX compatibility
CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2: an architecture-gated feature
study.depth: Explain eligibility only. Do not implement a cluster kernel in this unit.

focus: Check device availability and every query's return status before reading fields. Record compute capability, SM count, thread limits, shared-memory limits and compiled-kernel attributes.
A capability predicate, per-launch resource check and compatible code image are separate requirements. Device names and toolkit versions are not substitutes for those checks.
Build dispatch as a pure decision over queried facts and boundary facts, then launch only the selected legal path. Include an override that forces the baseline for differential testing.
Do not treat all CUDA errors as permission to retry another kernel. Invalid input or a failed execution can require reporting the error rather than continuing in a damaged context.
units.reproduce: Query `cudaGetDeviceProperties`, `cudaFuncGetAttributes` and the occupancy API for the baseline. Record `clusterLaunch` from the device properties as a feature-eligibility observation, not a cluster execution test. Implement a vector-copy selector requiring 16-byte-aligned pointers, compatible element type, a correctly handled tail and legal launch resources; otherwise choose the scalar grid-stride copy. Unit-test synthetic dispatch facts on the CPU, but launch only paths actually supported by the current device. Compare automatic dispatch and forced baseline on lengths 0, 1, 31, 32, 33 and 1025 and on offset views. Log the selected path and failed precondition. An unavailable device produces an explicit unsupported result, not a fabricated successful GPU run.
traps: Hard-coding a product-name whitelist. Similar names can have different limits and future devices are unknown to the list.
Forcing a synthetic supported capability into a real launch. Mocking tests the decision function, not hardware execution.
Equating PTX forward compatibility with unrestricted driver compatibility. The installed driver must understand the shipped PTX version and support the device.

selfTest.q: Does a legal thread count prove a kernel launch is legal?
selfTest.a: No. Registers, static plus dynamic shared memory, kernel-specific limits and other launch requirements also matter.

selfTest.q: How do you test an unavailable optimized branch honestly?
selfTest.a: Test its decision logic with synthetic facts and report execution as untested on this device. Run the baseline and any genuinely supported optimized paths against the reference.

selfTest.q: Does a feature-support query prove that the optimized path is faster?
selfTest.a: No. It proves eligibility for that feature, not performance. Choose a default only after representative correctness-checked measurements.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `kernellab` queried capability manifest, pure dispatch tests, automatic-versus-forced-baseline comparisons and explicit unsupported-feature report. Cluster execution is not required on unsupported hardware.
units.stopWhen: Your dispatch report explains every tested selection, both supported copy paths match the reference, and unavailable hardware paths are clearly separated from mocked decision tests.
